title: When I survey (Watts, 1707)
hook: love so amazing, so divine, demands my soul, my life, my all
carry: my soul, my life, my all
tomorrow: a hymn writer says his chains fell off. what chains?

segments.voice: Yesterday the covenant service: doing or suffering, full or empty, and one answer for both, I am thine. Today, hymns. The first one asks what you could ever give back.

Graduation cards with a check folded inside. A grandparent's watch handed down. A friend who drove four hours because you asked. Some gifts are too big to pay back, and the usual move, a matching gift, a thank-you note, feels small next to them. Isaac Watts wrote a hymn that runs straight into that feeling. In it, the whole world would be too small a gift. For what? He starts by asking you to look.
screen: `A GIFT TOO BIG TO PAY BACK.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD, TOO SMALL.` → `HE STARTS BY ASKING YOU TO LOOK.`

segments.voice: "When I survey the wondrous cross." Survey: look it over, slowly, the way you'd study a map. And what Watts sees reorders his accounts. His richest gain he counts as loss, an echo of Paul to the Philippians: "what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ." Then the picture at the center: "See from his head, his hands, his feet, Sorrow and love flow mingled down." Sorrow and love, not separable, in the same stream. Then the last verse, the one people know: "Were the whole realm of nature mine, That were a present far too small; Love so amazing, so divine, Demands my soul, my life, my all." That's the answer to the riddle. The whole world is too small a gift for that kind of love. Watts doesn't try to pay it back. He can't. So the response changes kind: not a present, a person. Not something I own, but my soul, my life, my all. Here's what that does on an ordinary Tuesday. When someone gives you more than you could ever return, the hymn suggests the answer isn't a matching gift. It's letting that love change how you live.
screen: `SURVEY: LOOK IT OVER, SLOWLY.` · `GAIN COUNTED AS LOSS.` · `SORROW AND LOVE FLOW MINGLED.` · `A PRESENT FAR TOO SMALL.` · then, large: `MY SOUL, MY LIFE, MY ALL.`

segments.voice: Find one thing someone gave you that you could never really repay: a card, a photo, a ring, a cross. Set it in front of you and look it over slowly, the way Watts surveys. Then read the last verse silently, one line per breath: were the whole realm of nature mine, that were a present far too small; love so amazing, so divine, demands my soul, my life, my all.
When I survey. Watts's hymn of looking at the cross until the whole world seems too small a gift.
Your line: my soul, my life, my all. Some love can't be repaid, only answered with a life. Day 1664, sung.

howItsDone: Churches of many traditions sing When I survey the wondrous cross, often in the days before Easter; some Christians read hymns slowly as prayers.

fork.setup: a neighbor shoveled your family's driveway all winter and won't take a dime. your dad wants to sneak cash into her mailbox. what does Watts's last verse suggest?
options: some gifts can't be paid back; they're answered by how you live.
pay her quietly anyway; love means keeping things even.
forget it; a free gift isn't worth thinking about.
fork.reveal: Watts writes that the whole realm of nature would be a present far too small. his answer isn't a matching gift; it's my soul, my life, my all.

original.note: Greek: cross, the word in the New Testament for what Watts surveys.

trapdoor: what you thought: a solemn old church song about the crucifixion.
what it means: a hymn about looking slowly, and a love so big that only a life can answer it.
what a scholar hears: 'gain counted loss' from Philippians 3:7; and the first verse was soon revised, which is why hymnals differ.

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (shape: life; Grace: Pop is home and gives her his cross pin for graduation).

Watts quoted in modernized spelling and capitals (the 1707 printing reads 'wond'rous' and capitalizes nouns). The second line differs between the first printing ('Where the young Prince of Glory dy'd') and later ones ('On which the Prince of glory died'); the voice avoids that line. Confirm.
Trapdoor floor 3 ('the first verse was soon revised, which is why hymnals differ'): confirm; no date given in the voice.
The Philippians 3:7 echo is a reading; Watts's own heading for the hymn cites Galatians 6:14. Confirm.
howItsDone: 'churches of many traditions ... often in the days before Easter' is a general claim; a Keeper may soften.
